fixes.explanation: Leviathan, baker. Asaph says to God, “You crushed the heads of Leviathan…” (Psalm 74:14) Then he says, “You fed him to the creatures of the desert.” (Psalm 74:14) That's the creature he names.

Stones don't show up in this verse, friend. Asaph calls the people “…the sheep of Your pasture?” (Psalm 74:1) Stones just sit there, and sheep need looking after. I think that's why the question stings.
Zion it is, friend. Asaph says it plainly: “…Mount Zion, where You dwell.” (Psalm 74:2) Right there in his prayer, he names the mountain.

I get why that sounds right, baker, but listen to what Asaph asks. He wants God to turn His steps to “the everlasting ruins, to everything in the sanctuary the enemy has destroyed.” (Psalm 74:3) He asks about everything the enemy destroyed there, not just a few things.

False is right, friend. Asaph asks God, “Turn Your steps to the everlasting ruins, to everything in the sanctuary the enemy has destroyed.” (Psalm 74:3) That's no couple of dents. He points God to everything the enemy destroyed there.

That's what the text says, baker. “They have burned Your sanctuary to the ground…” (Psalm 74:7) The psalm also tells of smashing the carvings with hatchets and picks. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to just let it be heavy.
False is right, friend. Asaph says, “They burned down every place where God met us in the land.” (Psalm 74:8) That's every place, with none left standing. It's a heavy line.
Taunt is the word, friend. “How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You?” (Psalm 74:10) Asaph brings that question straight to God.

Fear is a good word, baker, but Asaph didn't use it here. He asks, “How long, O God, will the enemy taunt You?” (Psalm 74:10) A taunt is an insult aimed at someone, and here it's aimed at God. The word that fits the blank is taunt.

I can see why you'd hesitate, friend, but this one is True. Asaph asks, “Will the foe revile Your name forever?” (Psalm 74:10) Revile means to insult, and the target is God's name. I think Asaph is hurting for the people and for God's name too.
A nice thought, friend, but it's not what Asaph asks here. He says, “Stretch it out to destroy them!” (Psalm 74:11) Blessing the land isn't what's on his lips in this line.
Behemoth is a good guess, friend, but Asaph doesn't name it here. He says, “You crushed the heads of Leviathan…” (Psalm 74:14) Leviathan is the creature in this verse.
The great fish is a different story, baker. That one swallowed Jonah the prophet (Jonah 1:17). Here Asaph says, “You crushed the heads of Leviathan…” (Psalm 74:14)
True, friend. Asaph says to God, “You dried up the ever-flowing rivers.” (Psalm 74:15) These are rivers that were ever-flowing, and the verse says He dried them up.
Praise is the opposite of what Asaph says, friend. He says, “…a foolish people has spurned Your name.” (Psalm 74:18) Spurned means turned away with scorn. The word that fits the blank is spurned.
Fear isn't the word Asaph uses, baker. He says, “…a foolish people has spurned Your name.” (Psalm 74:18) Spurned means they turned it away with scorn. That's the word that fits.
Covenant is right, baker. Asaph says, “Consider Your covenant…” (Psalm 74:20) A covenant is a binding promise, and he brings it right into his prayer. He's asking God to consider it.
The altar isn't in that verse, friend. Asaph says, “Consider Your covenant…” (Psalm 74:20) A covenant is a binding promise. That's what he asks God to consider.
Festivals sound like a fun answer, baker, but Asaph doesn't name them. He says, “Consider Your covenant…” (Psalm 74:20) A covenant is a binding promise, and that's what he asks God to consider.
Praise, baker. Asaph prays, “may the poor and needy praise Your name.” (Psalm 74:21) That's what he asks for the poor and needy. I think that's a good prayer for anyone.
